questions.stem: A 30-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by law enforcement officers after being found disoriented and agitated at a public place. questions.solutionHtml:
e Schedule (76 drugs and their derivatives are listed), e.g. Amphetamine, pentobarbital, psilocybine and diazepam.

Option A. Opium/Heroin: Is a narcotic drug derived from morphine, an opiate found in the poppy plant. It has a high potential for abuse and is regulated under the NDPS Act.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with symptoms of poisoning. He is conscious but in distress, and reports ingesting a substance about an hour ago. The medical officer notes a distinct smell from the patient's breath. Considering the nature of the substance ingested and the time since ingestion, the medical officer must decide on the appropriate decontamination procedure. questions.solutionHtml:
r="ltr" lang="EN" style="font-size:12.0pt">. Caustic potash: Like other strong alkalis, can cause perforation during lavage.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Understand the indications for gastric lavage in acute poisoning cases, especially its appropriateness in carbolic acid poisoning.

 

Contraindications for gastric lavage –

 

  • Corrosive poisoning (except carbolic acid) owing to danger of perforation (absolute contraindication).
  • Convulsant poison, as it may lead to convulsions (e.g. strychnine).
  • Comatose patients because of risk of aspiration into air-passages.
  • Volatile poisons and hydrocarbons (petroleum distillate and kerosene oil) which may cause aspiration pneumonitis.
  • Risk of hemorrhage or perforation due to esophageal or gastric pathology, like upper alimentary diseases (esophageal varices) or recent surgery.
  • Hypothermia or hemorrhagic diathesis.
  • Compromised unprotected airway.
  • Ingestion of a foreign body (e.g. drug packet).

 

Ref: Reddy 33/e. Pg 514-515, 516

questions.stem: A 42-year-old male is brought to a district hospital following suspected poisoning. The medical officer is assessing various treatment options to enhance the elimination of the ingested substance. The officer considers a method that involves inducing sweating. Which of the following substances is correctly categorized as being used for this purpose?
questions.solutionHtml:
Option A. Chelating agents: These bind to certain heavy metals in the body, aiding in their excretion via the urinary system, and are commonly used in cases of metal poisoning.

 

Option C. Purging: This refers to methods such as inducing vomiting or using laxatives to remove ingested poisons from the gastrointestinal tract.

 

Option D. Forced alkaline diuresis: This is a process where urine alkalization is used to increase the elimination of certain drugs (like salicylates and phenobarbital) from the body.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Diaphoretics (sudorifics): Application of heat (blankets or hot water bottles) and administration of warm beverages—alcohol, ipecac, pilocarpine, opium, sweet spirits of nitre and salicylates will cause increased perspiration and speeds up the excretion of toxic agents, but its usefulness is doubtful.

 

Note - These are not the primary treatments for heavy metal poisoning.

questions.stem: A medical officer at a district hospital is training new paramedics on the recognition of poisoning symptoms. During the training, the officer emphasizes the importance of observing pupil size as an indicator of certain types of poisoning. The medical officer presents a case scenario and asks: For which of the following poisonings is constricted pupil not a typical finding?
questions.solutionHtml:
:"Calibri",sans-serif">: Congestion of the GIT, centrilobular hepatic necrosis, acute tubular necrosis, cerebral edema and myocardial necrosis

 

Explanation:

 

Option B. Opium: Opium and its derivatives (opioids) characteristically cause miosis due to their action on the central nervous system.

 

Option C. Phenol: Exposure to phenol can also lead to miosis, although its primary toxic effects are corrosive.

 

Option D. Organophosphorus compounds (OPC): OPC poisoning leads to miosis due to the inhibition of acetylcholinesterase, resulting in an accumulation of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junctions, including those in the eyes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In the context of poisoning, constricted pupils are not typically associated with paracetamol poisoning, which primarily causes hepatotoxicity. In contrast, opium, phenol, and organophosphorus compounds are known to cause miosis as part of their toxicological effects. Recognizing this symptom can be crucial in the initial assessment and management of poisoning cases.

questions.stem: During a practical session, a forensic expert is demonstrating various types of poisonings to medical students using simulated cases. The expert discusses the mode of action of different poisons and how they affect the body. To test the students' understanding, the expert presents a scenario of a person who developed symptoms only at the point of contact after exposure to a substance, without showing any systemic signs. The question is “Which of the following poisons is known to act only locally without systemic effects?"
questions.solutionHtml:
ign:justify"> 

Option B. Carbolic acid: While carbolic acid also acts locally as a corrosive, it is more readily absorbed through the skin and can cause systemic toxicity. Phenol being fat-soluble, attacks the nervous system and causes paralysis of respiratory and CVS centers leading to death

 

Option C. Oxalic acid: It acts locally as a corrosive on both skin and mucosa, and remotely affects several systems after being absorbed –

 

  • CVS →shock → death
  • Electrolyte system → extracts tissue calcium →hypocalcemia
  • Renal system → tubular necrosis → uremia → death

 

Option D. Phosphorus: Phosphorus poisoning, especially white phosphorus, is known for its systemic effects as fat soluble, including hepatic and renal toxicity.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Medicolegal aspect of Vitriolage (Common acids - Sulphuric acid, Nitric acid and Hydrochloric acid) –

 

  • These fluids are usually thrown on the face with the object of destroying vision or causing facial disfigurement, and this results in grievous hurt (Sec. 320 IPC).
  • It is punishable under Sec. 326-A IPC (voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acids) for 10 years to life imprisonment and fine paid to the victim, and under Sec 326-B IPC (voluntarily throwing or attempting to throw acid) with imprisonment for 5-7 years and fine

questions.stem: A 30-year-old individual presents to the emergency department with severe pain, restlessness, hypertension, tachycardia, and sweating after being stung by a scorpion. The sting site is red and swollen, with no signs of necrosis. What is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient's condition?

options.label: B
options.text: Apply a tourniquet proximal to the sting site

options.label: D
options.text: Cleanse the wound and apply ice packs

questions.solutionHtml:
tyle="font-family:Arial,sans-serif">Cholinergic syndrome: Salivation, sweating, urinary incontinence, diarrhea), miosis, bronchospasm, bradycardia with hypotension and, priapism in males.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Administer antivenom immediately: Antivenom is given only in cases of severe envenomation with significant systemic symptoms, such as respiratory distress, cardiovascular instability etc.

 

Option B. Apply a tourniquet proximal to the sting site: Applying a tourniquet can worsen tissue damage, delay proper wound care, and increase the risk of complications.

 

Option D. Cleanse the wound and apply ice packs: For cases with mild local symptoms, wound cleansing to prevent infection and the application of ice packs or cold compresses to the sting site can help alleviate pain and reduce swelling. However, in cases of significant systemic symptoms like restlessness, hypertension, and tachycardia, addressing the autonomic effects with prazosin is more crucial. The wound care is secondary, and ice pack can be applied later on.

 

Note - While ice packs are recommended in scorpion bite, it is not to be given in snake bite. Snake venom can contain enzymes that cause tissue damage and affect blood circulation. Cold temperature can constrict blood vessels and worsen the local damage.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Management of Scorpion bite:

 

  • Cold compress or Ice pack
  • Prazosin therapy–a post-synaptic alpha1, adreno-receptor antagonist–is the first line of management. It suppresses sympathetic outflow.
  • Scorpion Antivenom: Anti-venom has to be given within 30 minutes of sting to be effective. So useful only in limited cases which present very early. Also, it is reserved for cases of severe envenomation only.

During the assessment, the medical officer observes that the patient's urine has turned green. This unusual symptom raises concerns about the specific toxic substance involved. Which toxic substance is most likely responsible for the green-colored urine seen in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
"text-align:justify">Option A. Lead: Lead poisoning usually lead to symptoms like abdominal pain, anemia, and neurological changes.

 

Option C. Organophosphorus: Organophosphorus compounds, primarily affecting the nervous system.

 

Option D. Cyanide: Cyanide poisoning, characterized by severe systemic effects such as respiratory failure and cardiac arrest

 

Educational Objective:

 

Green-colored urine as a potential indicator of phenol ingestion in cases of poisoning.

 

Some important Pointers related to Phenol Poisoning -

 

  • Postmortem Findings -
    • External: Grayish or brownish corrosions at the angle of the mouth, chin, front of the body, arms and hands with phenolic odor. Putrefaction is retarded.
    • Internal -
      • Corrosion of the GIT mucosa, and laryngeal and pulmonary edema.

      • Vomitus and gastric lavage collection show partially detached gastric mucosa.
      • Kidneys: Hemorrhagic nephritis.
  • Medico-legal Aspects - It is used for suicidal purposes; Accidental poisoning may occur; Phenol is rarely used for homicidal poisoning because of its odor and taste. Sometimes, it is used as an abortifacient.

On examination, he has hyperkeratosis of the skin and exhibits both sensory and motor deficits. His complete blood count reveals mild anemia. Considering chronic exposure in his workplace, which of the following conditions is least likely to be associated with this patient's chronic poisoning?
questions.solutionHtml:
span dir="ltr" lang="EN" style="font-size:12.0pt">Option A. Mixed sensory and motor neuropathy: Chronic arsenic exposure can lead to peripheral neuropathy, presenting as a combination of sensory and motor deficits due to nerve damage.

 

Option C. Hyperkeratosis of skin: Arsenic exposure can cause thickening of the skin, particularly on palms and soles, known as hyperkeratosis.

 

Option D. Anemia: Arsenic can interfere with red blood cell production, leading to anemia, a condition characterized by a reduced number of red blood cells.

 

Educational Objective:
 

Chronic arsenic poisoning - Sign and symptoms –

 

  • A metallic taste, excessive salivation, and garlic odor of breath and sweat may indicate chronic arsenic poisoning.
  • Melanosis and leucomelanosis with or without keratosis are the earliest symptoms of arsenicosis.
  • Chronic exposure also causes diabetes, vasospasm and peripheral vascular insufficiency (blackfoot disease—peripheral vascular disease characterized by systemic arteriosclerosis resulting in dry gangrene and spontaneous amputations of affected extremities).

 

Postmortem Findings

 

  • External: Emaciation, pigmentation, keratosis, alopecia, white streaks on nails, jaundice, wasting of muscles, and ulceration of nasal septum.
  • Internal -
    • Stomach: It may be normal or may show a chronic gastritis. Some rugae may show patchy inflammatory redness or focal ulceration.
    • Small intestine: Reddish with thickened mucosa.
    • Liver: Hepatomegaly, fatty degeneration or even necrosis with non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis.
    • Kidneys: Tubular necrosis.
    • Heart: Myocardial necrosis may be seen.
    • Bone marrow histopathology will show hypoplasia.

 

(If arsenic poisoning is suspected, hair or tissue samples should be obtained for confirmation.)

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is brought to a pediatric casualty medical officer with symptoms of irritability, photophobia, excessive sweating, and a pinkish discoloration of the hands and feet. Medical history reveals potential exposure to household items containing older preservatives. Given these clinical features, which poisoning is most likely responsible for the condition known as acrodynia, or Pink disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
ea.

 

 

Explanation:

 

Option B. Arsenic: Causes skin changes like raindrop pigmentation, palmer hyperkeratosis, vasospasm and peripheral vascular insufficiency leads to blackfoot disease resulting in dry gangrene and spontaneous amputations of affected extremities, but not cause acrodynia.
 

Option C. Lead: Lead poisoning can result in neurological and hematological manifestations, but not in acrodynia. The clinical features are abdominal pain, irritability, lethargy, anorexia, anemia, Fanconi’s syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, pyuria and azotemia in children. Additionally, headaches, arthralgias, myalgias, depression, impaired short term memory, and loss of libido in adults. The blue line on the gums is a valuable but variable clue to diagnosis.

 

Option D. Thallium: Known for causing alopecia (brownish black pigmentation close to the hair root, appear as early as 3rd–4th day ) and neuropathic pain, but not acrodynia. GIT and polyneuritis symptoms together with the falling of hair from head, eyebrows and axilla should lead to suspicion of thallium poisoning.

 

Educational Objective:
 

Acrodynia, or Pink disease, is a rare condition typically seen in children and is characterized by symptoms such as irritability, photophobia, excessive sweating, and pink discoloration of the hands and feet. This condition is primarily associated with mercury poisoning, often from exposure to mercury-containing compounds in the environment or household items.

questions.solutionHtml:
High anion gap acidosis: Typically associated with conditions like methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning, not copper sulfate poisoning.

questions.stem: In a case of heavy metal poisoning, the emergency department team is considering the use of British Anti-Lewisite (BAL) as a chelating agent. Understanding the specific indications for BAL is crucial for effective treatment. For which of the following heavy metal poisonings is BAL not indicated?
questions.solutionHtml:
n>. Lead: BAL is effective.

 

Option B. Mercury: BAL is used as a chelator.

 

Option D. Arsenic: BAL is indicated for arsenic poisoning.

 

Educational Objective:

 

BAL (British anti-lewisite, dimercaprol):

 

  • It is used in arsenic, lead, bismuth, copper, mercury, gold and other heavy metal poisoning.
  • Many heavy metals have affinity for sulfhydryl (–SH) radicals, combine with them in tissues and deprive the body of the use of respiratory enzymes. BAL has two unsaturated –SH groups which combine with the metal and thus prevent the union of the metal with the –SH group of the respiratory enzyme system.
  • Dose: 10% solution in oil, 3–5 mg/kg IM 4 hourly for 2 days, 6 hourly on 3rd day and then 12 hourly for next 10 days.
  • Side effects: Nausea, vomiting, headache and hypertension.
  • Contraindicated in liver damage, G-6-PD deficient individuals, and cadmium and iron poisoning (since dimercaprol-cadmium and dimercaprol-iron complex is itself toxic).

bles Guillain-Barre polyneuritis. Ideal homicidal poison. Pseudo motor neuropathy is seen.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Lead poisoning: Presents with gastrointestinal, neurological, and hematological symptoms, but lacks the rapid progression and specific combination of symptoms seen in thallium poisoning.
 

Option B. Mercury poisoning: Known for neurological effects, particularly tremors, but the symptom profile does not match precisely with this case.
 

Option D. Arsenic poisoning: Arsenic and Thallium have very similar features. The main features because of which thallium is preferred over arsenic are:

  • Alopecia and Madarosis: Thallium causes severe alopecia and madarosis (loss of eyebrows), often early. Arsenic can cause alopecia, but madarosis is rare and less severe.
  • Neurological Effects: Thallium causes acute neurological symptoms (encephalopathy, delirium, convulsions, coma, peripheral neuropathy). Arsenic mainly causes neuropathy with less severe neurological symptoms.
  • Progression: Thallium has rapid, acute progression leading to death without treatment. Arsenic typically causes chronic toxicity with long-term effects like skin changes and cancer..

 

Educational Objective:


Thallium triad is characterized by alopecia, skin rashes, painful peripheral neuropathy and mental confusion with lethargy.

 

Sign de sourcil: "The eyebrow sign" (outer 2/3rd of eyebrow falls) the characteristics of thallium poisoning.

 

Note - Both thallium and arsenic have many similar features (both have Mees lines, peripheral neuropathies, GI symptoms, skin symptoms etc..). But the key differentiating feature is that, thallium is associated more with alopecia, whereas, arsenic more with GI symptoms.

Bites would show symptoms within the first 6 hr.  Victims wake up later, paralyzed or die in their sleep.

Krait venom is highly potent, and a dose as low as 6 mg can be lethal in humans. The venom contains neurotoxins that lead to paralysis by blocking neurotransmitter release at the neuromuscular junction.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male is admitted to a district hospital following a snakebite. He was working in his field when he felt a sudden sharp pain in his leg. On examination, the medical officer notes significant swelling and blistering around the bite site, extending up the leg. The patient also shows signs of systemic involvement, including altered mental status and difficulty breathing. Given the severity of the envenomation, what is the initial dose of antivenom that should be administered?
questions.solutionHtml:
serif">Ans. C) 10 vials

 

Explanation:

 

The lyophilized polyvalent antisnake venom (ASV) serum: This serum is effective against common poisonous snakes in India, including cobra, common krait, saw-scaled viper, and Russell's viper.

 

Dose Administration: The ASV is freeze-dried and dissolved in water, typically a 10 ml vial. Around 100 ml of this serum should be diluted in 200-500 ml of isotonic saline for slow intravenous (IV) administration.

 

Recommended Initial Dose:  The initial dose of ASV is recommended to be 10 vials, administered via IV over about 1 hour.

 

Repeat Doses: For vasculotoxic species (like Russell's viper), repeat doses depend on the 6-hour rule, guided by the coagulation profile, with a maximum recommended dose of 30 vials. For neurotoxic species (like cobra and krait), the repeat dose is based on a 1–2-hour rule, depending on patient improvement or worsening, with a maximum dose of 20 vials.

 

Indications for Antivenom: Systemic envenoming (e.g., spontaneous bleeding, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, CNS symptoms like ptosis, paralysis, CVS symptoms like hypotension, and acute renal failure), and local envenoming (e.g., swelling involving more than half of the bitten limb, rapid extension of swelling, enlarged tender lymph nodes).

 

Urgency and Contraindications: Antivenom treatment should be administered as soon as indicated. There are no absolute contraindications to ASV treatment. However, it should not be used indiscriminately due to risks of severe adverse reactions, cost, and limited supply.

 

Observation Post-Administration: Patients must be closely observed for at least 1 hour after starting IV antivenom to detect early anaphylactic reactions.

 

Dosing for Children: Children should receive the same dose of ASV as adults, as snakes inject the same amount of venom into both children and adults.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The initial dosing of antivenom in severe snake envenomation should be sufficient to neutralize the venom effectively. A starting dose of 10 vials is recommended in cases with significant systemic involvement, followed by careful monitoring and additional doses as needed. The goal is to use the minimum effective amount of antivenom to reduce the risk of adverse reactions while ensuring effective treatment.

"> 

Option A. Type II hypersensitivity reactions: These are antibody-mediated reactions against cell surface or matrix antigens, which is not the typical mechanism of ASV reactions.

 

Option C. Type IV hypersensitivity reactions: Also known as delayed-type hypersensitivity, these reactions involve T-cell-mediated responses and are not commonly associated with ASV.

 

Option D. Type V hypersensitivity reactions: This category, which includes stimulatory hypersensitivity, is not a mechanism associated with ASV reactions.

Antivenom reactions:

Adrenaline, 0.5–1.0 ml of 0.1% solution (1 in 1000, 1 mg/ml) is given subcutaneously in adults; in children the dose is 0.01 ml/kg.
  • Serum sickness is a type III (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction which is characterized by fever, urticaria, lymphadenopathy and arthritis, and may develop in 3 days to 3 weeks. Serum sickness is dose-related, as it occurs when > 8 vials of polyvalent ASV are administered.

questions.stem: In a forensic toxicology lab, a technician is conducting a test to identify the presence of a specific substance in a sample from a poisoning case. The technician uses the Marquis test, which is a colorimetric test known for its specific reaction. This test is particularly used for detecting which type of poisoning?
questions.solutionHtml:
rong> to presumptively identify alkaloids. It can be used to test cocaine, opiates and phenethylamines.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Mercury poisoning: Acute mercury poisoning can be detected by measuring blood levels (> 10 μg/dl), whereas urine ( > 20 μg/l) and hair (>5 ppm) analysis help confirming chronic exposure. Urine and blood mercury levels are assessed by atomic absorption spectrophotometer. Mercury concentration of hair is best assessed by neutron activation analysis.

 

Option B. Arsenic poisoning: Detected through urine excretion (> 50 μg/l in 24 h) of arsenic or metabolites of arsenic including methylarsonic acid and dimethylarsenic acid; Blood (serum arsenic > 0.9 μg/dl), stool, liver, kidneys and bones also shows the presence of arsenic. As with all heavy metals, microcytic hypochromic anemia is common. Hair (Arsenic > 75 μg%) and Nails (> 100 μg%) is suggestive of poisoning.

 

Option D. Cyanide poisoning: The triad of lab findings is suggestive of cyanide poisoning:

 

  1. A narrow arterial-venous oxygen difference
  2. An anion gap metabolic acidosis
  3. An elevated lactate concentration.

 

Measurement of whole blood cyanide in an anticoagulant tube (not done with plasma or serum since cyanide is sequestered in RBCs) can confirm toxicity. HCN is also measured by gas chromatography or spectrophotometry.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Marquis test is a colorimetric reagent test used primarily to detect the presence of alkaloids, particularly morphine and other opioids. When the Marquis reagent is added to a substance containing these opioids, it produces a distinct color change, which is a positive indication of their presence.

f">Explanation:

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male presents with a constellation of neurological symptoms, including alteration in mental function, VIth nerve palsy, and ataxia. These symptoms are concerning Wernicke's encephalopathy. Which of the following symptoms is NOT typically associated with Wernicke's encephalopathy?
questions.solutionHtml:
n style="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Ans. A) Cogwheel rigidity

 

Explanation:

 

Wernicke’s Encephalopathy - This is an acute reaction due to severe thiamine deficiency (Vit. B1), the commonest cause being chronic alcohol abuse. Characteristically, the onset occurs after a period of persistent vomiting.

 

Signs and Symptom

 

  1. Ocular: Coarse nystagmus and opthalmoparesis (usually the VIth cranial nerve is involved). Pupillary irregularity, retinal hemorrhages, papilledema and impairment of vision.
  2. CNS: Disorientation, confusion, recent memory disturbances, poor attention span and distractibility. Apathy and ataxia are early symptoms.
  3. Peripheral neuropath  and serious malnutrition are often coexistent.
  4. Pathologically, neuronal degeneration and hemorrhage is seen in the thalamus, hypothalamus (mammillary bodies) and midbrain.

 

Cogwheel rigidity may be seen in associated with other extrapyramidal manifestation of Organophosphorus poisoning. It develops in 4–40 days following poisoning and lasts for about 1-4 weeks.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Wernicke's encephalopathy is characterized by a triad of symptoms, including alteration in mental function (confusion), ophthalmoplegia (paralysis of eye muscles), and ataxia (loss of muscle coordination). VIth nerve palsy (involvement of the sixth cranial nerve) can result in difficulty moving the eyes laterally, leading to double vision and cogwheel rigidity is not a characteristic feature.

In evaluating patients with a history of chronic alcoholism, the presence of confabulation is a key clinical indicator of Korsakoff's psychosis. Recognizing this symptom is important for medical officers, as it aids in the differential diagnosis of neuropsychiatric disorders and guides appropriate treatment and management strategies.

dir="ltr" lang="EN" style="font-size:12.0pt">Option A. Periventricular gray matter: This area is commonly involved in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, a neuropsychiatric condition associated with thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, often seen in chronic alcoholics. t-align:justify">Option A. Alcoholic intoxication: While it can lead to confusion and motor incoordination, the other anticholinergic symptoms like dry mouth and dilated pupils are not typical.

Additionally, diminished bowel movements, distention of urinary bladder, Increased respiration, Scarlatiniform rash over the body, Amnesia and death due to respiratory failure.

 

Additional Information –

 

Treatment of Dhatura Poisoning –

 

  • Emetics.
  • Gastric lavage with tannic acid, KMnO4 or activated charcoal. First dose of activated charcoal may be given with cathartic (e.g. sorbitol). One or two additional doses may be given at 1–2 h intervals to ensure adequate gut decontamination.
  • Physiological antidote: Physostigmine salicylate (reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor capable of directly antagonizing CNS manifestations of anticholinergic toxicity) 0.5–1 mg slow IV over 5 min with ECG monitoring (0.02 mg/kg/dose).
  • Pilocarpine 5–15 mg subcutaneously is also useful.
  • Purgatives and colonic lavage is recommended.
  • Tepid sponge baths to control high temperature, and diazepam IV for sedation and seizures. Morphine is avoided.
  • Delirium is controlled by short acting barbiturates.
  • O2 inhalation and artificial respiration.
  • Hemodialysis and hemoperfusion are generally ineffective (tropane alkaloids are lipophilic and cross the blood-brain barrier).
  • Catheterization in case of urinary retention.
  • Moistening of the tongue and change in the size of pupils point towards normalization and are useful as guidelines for adequate management.

Additional Information –

 

Treatment of Strychnine Poisoning –

 

Treatment involves supportive care with minimization of external stimulus and prevention of convulsions.

 

  • Maintain clear airway and adequate ventilation including endotracheal intubation.
  • Control of convulsions: Dark room, free from noise and disturbance. Diazepam 0.1–0.5 mg/kg IV slowly. If ineffective, general anesthetics and/or muscle relaxants, like gallamine should be given.
  • Barbiturates, like pentobarbital sodium or sodium amytal are antidotes. Dose: 300–600 mg IV.
  • Gastric lavage with KMnO4 may be done cautiously, if there are no convulsions. Activated charcoal is recommended as it adsorbs strychnine and may reduce its absorption if given 1 hr of ingestion.
  • Hyperthermia is treated by active cooling with ice water immersion, cooling blanket or mist and fan.
  • Intravenous fluid is given to maintain a urine output > 1 ml/kg/hr, since metabolic acidosis and renal failure may occur. (Hemodialysis is not effective).
  • Symptomatic treatment.

questions.stem: A medical officer in a district hospital performs an autopsy on a suspected case of poisoning. The deceased had a history of consuming contaminated substances. Considering arsenic as the suspected poison, where would the greatest concentration of arsenic likely be found in the body?
questions.solutionHtml:
pan style="font-size:12.0pt;">Explanation:

 

Option A. Muscle: Although arsenic can be found in muscles if life is prolonged, it is not the primary site of accumulation in the early stages of poisoning. Over time, arsenic can be deposited in muscles, but initially, higher concentrations are found in the liver, kidneys, and spleen.

 

Option B. Kidney: The kidneys, along with the liver and spleen, are among the organs where arsenic accumulates in significant amounts in the early stages. However, the liver generally has a higher concentration than the kidneys.

 

Option D. Brain: Arsenic does not cross the blood-brain barrier effectively, resulting in lower levels in the brain compared to other organs. It does, however, cross the placenta.

 

Educational Objective:


Arsenic accumulates predominantly in the liver due to its role in metabolism and detoxification. In cases of arsenic poisoning, the liver often shows the highest concentration of the toxin.

r="ltr" lang="EN" style="font-size:12.0pt">Treatment: Supportive measures, since it does not respond to oximes or atropine.

an>

Educational Objective:

 

Appropriate management of iron poisoning - Treatment is usually whole-bowel irrigation and chelation therapy.

 

  • Fluid resuscitation: Normal saline drip or lactated Ringer's solution.
  • Decontamination: Gastric lavage or whole bowel irrigation with normal saline or polyethylene glycol-electrolyte solution.
  • Chelation therapy: Desferrioxamine (antidote)

questions.stem: During a seminar, a forensic expert discusses the concept of tolerance in substance abuse. Tolerance refers to the phenomenon where increasingly larger doses of a substance are required to achieve the same effect due to the body's adaptation to the drug. The expert presents a list of substances to the attendees and asks which one does not typically lead to the development of tolerance. Which of the following substances is known not to exhibit tolerance?
questions.solutionHtml:
font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Cocaine is known for not typically leading to tolerance development like other substances such as morphine, amphetamines, or barbiturates.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Morphine: Incorrect. Tolerance develops to morphine, an opioid, with repeated use. Actually, both morphine and heroine are dependence producing derivatives. Heroin is more addictive than morphine and can cause dependence after a short period of exposure. Tolerance to heroin occurs rapidly and can be increased to more than 100 times the first dose needed.

 

Option B. Amphetamine: Incorrect. Chronic use leads to severe compulsive craving for the drug and a high degree of tolerance (needs 15–20 times the initial dose to obtain the same effect). Tolerance usually develops to the CNS as well as CVS effects of amphetamines.

 

Option D. Barbiturates: Incorrect. Barbiturates produce marked physical and psychological dependence. Tolerance develops rapidly and is usually marked. There is also a cross-tolerance with alcohol.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cocaine does not typically lead to tolerance development, unlike opioids, stimulants, and barbiturates.

The parents mention that the child often plays in a nearby scrapyard. On examination, the child appears listless, with a noticeable pallor and mild abdominal distension. No hepatosplenomegaly is detected. A complete blood count reveals a hemoglobin level of 9.5 g/dL. A peripheral blood smear is performed, which demonstrates a peculiar finding shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: B

questions.solutionHtml:
g>, but basophilic stippling is not a characteristic feature of viral infections.

 

Option B. Lead poisoning leads to abnormal iron metabolism, leading to intracellular iron accumulation within RBCs. She is unresponsive to verbal stimuli and is breathing very shallowly. Friends who were with her mention that she had been using drugs at a party earlier. Her breathing rate is 6 breaths per minute, and her pupils are constricted. Her skin is pale, and she feels cool to the touch. Which of the following substances is most likely responsible for her presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
an style="font-size:11pt">Pupil size depression (Miosis, pinpoint pupil)

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Alcohol: Alcohol is also a CNS depressant, but the depressive effects are less severe as compared to opium poisoning. The pupils are usually dilated in alcohol poisoning; they become contracted only in late stages of alcohol poisoning.

 

Option B. Cocaine: It is a stimulant, not a depressant. So, the effects will be opposite. Cocaine poisoning will have dilated pupils. Breathing is rapid and shallow in cocaine but slow and shallow in opium poisoning. Also instead of unconsciousness, the person will be usually in heightened alertness.

 

Option D. Methaphmetamine: It is also a stimulant drug, and will have features somewhat similar to cocaine.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a history of recurrent epistaxis and difficulty breathing through his nose. He admits to a long-standing habit of drug use. On physical examination, the nasal speculum reveals septal ulceration and a perforation, as shown in the image provided. The feature shown in the image can occur in which poisoning?
questions.solutionHtml:
alt="" src="https://cerebellum-web-static.s3.amazonaws.com/media/public/images/2024/03/06/screenshot-2024-03-06-171322.jpg" style="height:367px; width:400px" />

 

Explanation:

 

Option B. Cannabis: Cannabis, derived from the Cannabis sativa plant, is typically consumed by smoking or ingestion. It is not associated with nasal septum ulceration or perforation. Its use can lead to various psychological and some physical effects, but it does not cause the direct local tissue damage seen with cocaine use through snorting.

 

Option C. Opium: Opium is extracted from the poppy plant (Papaver somniferum) and contains morphine, among other alkaloids. It can be ingested or smoked, but like cannabis, it does not cause ulceration or perforation of the nasal septum as it is not typically insufflated.

 

Option D. Arsenic: Arsenic poisoning usually occurs through ingestion or inhalation of arsenic-contaminated substances. Chronic arsenic exposure can lead to systemic symptoms and signs such as gastrointestinal distress, cardiac issues, skin changes, and neurological symptoms. It does not cause local damage to the nasal septum like cocaine.

 

In summary, cocaine is the only substance among the options provided that is commonly insufflated (snorted), leading to local nasal damage, which can manifest as ulceration and potential perforation of the nasal septum.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Cocaine is Obtained from leaves of Erythroxylon coca
  • Mode of Intake: a) Snorting b) Chewing coca leaves c) Smoking d) IV
  • Due to snorting, it can cause Ulceration and rarely perforation of nasal septum

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male with no significant past medical history is brought to the emergency department by his friends who report that he was acting increasingly erratic at a party. The patient is agitated, showing signs of paranoia, and is unable to sit still for the examination. Vital signs reveal a heart rate of 130 bpm, blood pressure of 160/100 mm Hg, and a respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute. Physical examination notes dilated pupils, diaphoresis, and elevated body temperature. What is the most likely cause of the patient's presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
tyle="text-align:justify">Seizures, Confusion and Altered Mental Status

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Acute Opioid overdose: Respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils, and decreased heart rate and blood pressure.

 

Option B  Acute Benzodiazepine overdose: Respiratory depression, and drowsiness.

 

Option D. Acute Alcohol intoxication: slurred speech, impaired coordination, and depressed consciousness.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Acute Cocaine Poisoning –

 

  • Signs and symptoms include elevated pulse, blood pressure, respiration and temperature. Onset occurs within 7 seconds after inhalation, 15 seconds after taking IV, 3 minutes (min) after nasal insufflations and 10 min after oral ingestion.
  • The initial stimulatory effects (rush) are followed by depression (crush).
  • Fatal dose: 20 mg IV; 500 mg to 1.2 g orally.
  • Fatal period: Few minutes to 1–2 h.

 

Ref: Reddy 33/e. Pg 602

questions.stem: During the autopsy of a 40-year-old man who had a sudden and unexplained death, a forensic expert conducts a thorough toxicological analysis. The man was previously healthy with no known chronic illnesses. His body shows no signs of trauma, but there is evidence of multi-organ failure. Tissue samples are collected for heavy metal analysis because of a suspected case of poisoning. The forensic expert is aware that arsenic has a specific distribution pattern in the body. In which of the following organs would the forensic expert least expect to find a significant concentration of arsenic?
questions.solutionHtml:
t-align:justify"> 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Liver: The liver is a common site for the deposition of arsenic due to its role in filtration and metabolism. Arsenic is processed in the liver where it binds to the cells, making it one of the organs with higher concentrations of arsenic during a toxicological analysis in an autopsy.

 

Option C. Skin: Arsenic has an affinity for keratin-rich tissues. The skin, which is high in keratin, often shows significant levels of arsenic in cases of poisoning. Additionally, skin manifestations such as hyperkeratosis and pigmentation changes can be seen with chronic arsenic exposure.

 

Option D. Bones: Arsenic can also be deposited in bones where it can persist for a long time. The detection of arsenic in bone tissue can be an indicator of long-term exposure and is relevant in forensic analysis because of the bone's ability to retain arsenic even after other tissues have been depleted.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Toxicokinetic of Arsenic:

 

  1. Because of short half-life of arsenic in the blood, arsenic is rapidly cleared from the blood. Hence it is less reliable to detect arsenic poisoning.
  2. after clearing from blood, arsenic gets deposited in almost all the tissues where it is found for prolonged period. However, arsenic does not cross blood brain barrier.
  3. Highest concentration is found in liver (followed by kidney)
  4. Urine becomes positive within 6 hours of poisoning and may continue to be positive for about 2-3 weeks. Urine is better than blood to detect arsenic poisoning.
  5. Arsenic also gets deposited in hair, nails, skin and bones where it remains for a much more prolonged time (even for years) after exposure.

 

Ref: Reddy 33/e. Pg 541

questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient presents with complaints of pain, numbness, and darkening of the lower extremities. Physical examination reveals gangrene in the feet and lower legs. The patient reports a history of residing in an area with known arsenic-contaminated drinking water. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for the patient's presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
le="font-family:Arial,sans-serif">Below picture shows Blackfoot disease

 

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Deep vein thrombosis involves the formation of blood clots in deep veins, typically in the legs. While it can cause pain and swelling, it does not lead to the specific pattern of darkening and necrosis seen in Blackfoot disease.

 

Option C. Raynaud's phenomenon is characterized by episodes of reduced blood flow to the fingers and toes, causing them to turn white, then blue, and then red. Gangrene is not a typical manifestation of Raynaud's phenomenon.

 

Option D. Diabetic neuropathy involves nerve damage due to diabetes, leading to symptoms such as pain, numbness, and tingling in the extremities. While diabetes can contribute to peripheral artery disease and related complications, the specific presentation of gangrene is more indicative of Blackfoot disease in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Blackfoot disease is a peripheral vascular disease resulting from chronic exposure to arsenic, which is known to contaminate drinking water in certain geographic areas. It is characterized by the progressive development of gangrene, usually in the lower extremities, leading to blackening (hence the name "Blackfoot"), severe pain, and numbness due to ischemia and subsequent necrosis. The condition can eventually necessitate amputation.

questions.stem: A hiker in a forested area is bitten by a snake while exploring. Hiker begins to experience symptoms such as swelling, pain, and bruising at the bite site. The hiker remains conscious but is anxious. What is the most appropriate initial first aid response for this snake bite?

options.label: A
options.text: Applying a tourniquet above the bite site to restrict blood flow and prevent venom spread.

options.label: B
options.text: Cutting open the wound and attempting to suck out the venom.

options.label: C
options.text: Immobilizing the affected limb at or slightly below heart level and transporting the person to a medical facility.

options.label: D
options.text: Applying ice packs directly to the bite area to reduce swelling and pain.

questions.answerText: Immobilizing the affected limb at or slightly below heart level and transporting the person to a medical facility.
questions.solutionHtml:
ption A. Applying a tourniquet above the bite site to restrict blood flow and prevent venom spread. It can lead to gangrene.

 

Option B. Cutting open the wound and attempting to suck out the venom. It can introduce infections, increase absorption of the venom and increase local bleeding.

 

Option D. Applying ice packs directly to the bite area to reduce swelling and pain. While ice packs are recommended in scorpion bite, it is not to be given in snake bite. Snake venom can contain enzymes that cause tissue damage and affect blood circulation. Cold temperature can constrict blood vessels and worsen the local damage.

The child is alert and oriented, with stable vital signs. Physical examination reveals a localized swelling of less than 5 centimeters in diameter on the child's leg, but no systemic signs of envenoming such as bleeding, ptosis, or hypotension are present. Laboratory investigations, including coagulation tests, are within normal limits except for the presence of the swelling. What is the next step in the management of this patient?

options.label: D
options.text: Observe the patient for progression of symptoms wait for anti-venom therapy

    Option A. Perform incision and suction of the local swelling: This practice is not recommended as it can increase the risk of infection and cause further tissue damage without effectively removing venom. Modern snakebite management does not include incision and suction as part of the treatment protocol due to the potential for harm and lack of evidence for benefit.

     

    Option B. Administer intravenous antivenom serum: Antivenom is indicated when there are signs of systemic envenoming or severe local envenoming. In this case, without systemic symptoms or laboratory evidence of envenoming, immediate administration of antivenom is not warranted due to the risks of allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, and serum sickness.

     

    Option C. Inject subcutaneous antivenom at the site of the local swelling: There is no role for local administration of antivenom, and it is not a recommended practice. Antivenom is administered intravenously because it needs to enter systemic circulation to neutralize venom components effectively.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious in a warehouse. On examination, he exhibits signs of respiratory distress, blurred vision, and metabolic acidosis. His companions suspect he may have ingested a substance found in the warehouse. After initial stabilization and laboratory investigations, the diagnosis of methanol poisoning is made based on his history and clinical presentation. Which of the following is NOT an appropriate treatment for methanol poisoning in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
, and salicylates, where alkalinization of urine enhances the excretion of the toxin.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Ethanol and Option B. Fomepizole are competitive inhibitors of alcohol dehydrogenase, the enzyme responsible for metabolizing methanol into its toxic metabolites, formic acid, and formaldehyde. By inhibiting this enzyme, these agents prevent the formation of the toxic metabolites, making them effective treatments for methanol poisoning.

 

Option C. Hemodialysis is effective in removing methanol and its toxic metabolites from the blood, especially in severe cases or when the patient presents with significant metabolic acidosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

 Treatment of Methanol Poisoning

 

  1. Stomach wash with sodium bicarbonate (please remember that Activated charcoal is not used in methanol poisoning as it does not not adsorb Alcohols)
  2. Antidotes: Ethanol or 4 methyl pyrazole (fomepizole) can be used. They preferentially compete with methyl alcohol for the same enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase and prevents the metabolism of methanol which is then excreted unchanged in the urine.
  3. Sodium bicarbonate IV: For acidosis
  4. Folinic acid IV: It hastens the elimination of formic acid. Folinic acid is a biologically active form of folic acid.
  5. For convulsions: Initially give benzodiazepine (diazepam or lorazepam). If seizures persist administer phenobarbitone.
  6. Hemodialysis: Strongly recommended in patients with acidosis or serum methanol levels of greater than 25 to 50 mg/100 ml.

 

Hemoperfusion is not effective. Peritoneal dialysis and continuous venovenous hemofiltration are less effective.

 

Ref: Reddy 33/e. Pg 582-583

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of working in a battery recycling plant presents to the clinic with complaints of persistent tremors, difficulty with coordination, and occasional episodes of slurred speech. He mentions that these symptoms have been gradually worsening over the past year. On examination, you observes involuntary coarse tremor predominantly in the hands, which intensifies when he attempts to perform tasks or extend his arms. Given the patient's occupational history and clinical presentation, you suspect chronic exposure to a heavy metal. Which of the following heavy metal poisonings is most likely associated with the characteristic tremor observed in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
t-family:Arial,sans-serif">Option A. Lead poisoning typically presents with gastrointestinal symptoms, anemia, neuropathy, and cognitive dysfunction, but not with the fine tremor’s characteristic of mercury exposure.

 

Option C. Arsenic poisoning can cause skin changes, peripheral neuropathy, and gastrointestinal symptoms, but it does not typically present with tremors.

 

Option D. Thallium poisoning is known for causing severe hair loss (alopecia), painful neuropathies, and gastrointestinal symptoms, but not the specific type of tremor associated with mercury poisoning.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Intention tremors (Danbury tremors/shaking palsy)

 

  • It occurs first in the hands, then progresses to the lips and tongue, and finally involves the arms and legs.
  • Tremor is moderately coarse and is interspersed by jerky movements. The patient may not display much tremor during an accustomed job, but if he is being observed, he may begin to shake violently.
  • In the advanced stage, the person is unable to dress himself, write legibly or walk properly. They are also called hatter’s shakes or glass blower’s shakes, as they are common in persons working with mercury in glass-blowing and hat industries.
  • The most severe form of tremors is known as concussion mercurilis.

 

Other compounds causing tremors: Alcohol; Phosphorus; Phenothiazines; Carbon monoxide; Antidepressants (tricyclic); Caffeine and theophylline

 

Ref: Reddy 33/e. Pg 543

questions.solutionHtml:

Explanation:

 

Option A. The leaf of the poppy plant does not contain significant amounts of opiate substances.

 

Option B. The root of the poppy plant is not the source of opium.

 

Option C. While poppy seeds can contain trace amounts of opiates due to contamination from other parts of the poppy plant, they are not a direct source of opium.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Opium - Toxic part: Unripe fruit capsule, latex juice.

 

  • Latex is obtained by lacerating (‘scoring’) the immature seed pods; the latex leaks out and dries to a sticky brown residue. This is scraped off the fruit.
  • Seeds are non-poisonous and are called ‘khaskhas’ which constitutes a condiment in cooking.
  • Active Principles - The latex juice of opium has about 25 alkaloids, divided into two groups: Phenanthrene derivatives (main narcotic constituents) and Benzyl-isoquinolone derivatives (no significant CNS effects).

 

Note - Opium disappears with putrefaction, so it may not be detected in putrefied bodies.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male presents to the emergency department with agitation, mydriasis, and profuse sweating. He reports a history of substance abuse and mentions recent use of a white powdery substance at a party. On examination, his vital signs are elevated, and he is experiencing palpitations. What is the most likely substance responsible for his current clinical presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
otent stimulant that leads to increased sympathetic activity. Clinical features of acute cocaine intoxication include agitation, mydriasis, elevated vital signs (tachycardia), and profuse sweating.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. MDMA (Ecstasy): MDMA (Methylene-dioxy-methamphetamine or ecstasy or Molly) is similar to mescaline and also known as one of the 'club drugs' or ‘rave drug’. It is a stimulant with hallucinogenic properties, supposed to interact with serotoninergic neurons in the CNS (typical effects include increased empathy and sensory perception). It is less likely to cause marked agitation and mydriasis compared to cocaine.

 

Option B. Marijuana: Marijuana use is associated with relaxation, euphoria, and altered perception. It is unlikely to cause the marked agitation and sympathetic overactivity seen in the patient.

 

Option D. Heroin: Heroin is an opioid and typically causes sedation, respiratory depression, and constricted pupils (miosis). It does not typically produce the sympathetic overactivity seen with cocaine use.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The characteristic clinical features of acute cocaine intoxication, includes agitation, mydriasis, elevated vital signs, and profuse sweating.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old worker in a wastewater treatment plant presents to the emergency department with complaints of headache, nausea, and confusion. He reports exposure to a foul-smelling gas while working in a confined space. On examination, the patient has a "rotten egg" odor on his breath, and his vital signs are stable. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
amily:Arial,sans-serif">

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Carbon monoxide poisoning: Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless gas, and exposure is often associated with combustion processes. Symptoms include headache and confusion, but carbon monoxide does not produce a "rotten egg" odor. Carbon monoxide poisoning is usually suspected when there is exposure to sources like faulty heating systems.

 

Option C. Cyanide toxicity: Cyanide exposure can occur in various industrial settings, and symptoms include confusion, nausea, and respiratory distress. However, cyanide does not produce a "rotten egg" odor, instead it has bitter almond odor.

 

Option D. Ammonia inhalation: Ammonia exposure can cause respiratory symptoms, eye irritation, and cough. It does not typically produce a "rotten egg" odor. Ammonia is commonly used in refrigeration systems and cleaning products.
